title: The Growth of Grassroots Resistance Movements Within the United States
author: Eric Toussaint
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/IMG_3641-680x510.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/28/the-
growth-of-grassroots-resistance-movements-within-the-united-states/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/03/IMG_3641-680x510.jpg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

One of the key factors in understanding Donald Trump’s foreign policy is not
to view the United States as a homogeneous bloc standing united behind its
president. Throughout his first term (2017–2021) and his second term, which
began in January 2025, Trump has faced internal resistance on a considerable
scale. This resistance has taken many forms: mass mobilisations, trade union
action, election campaigns, international solidarity movements, civil
disobedience and the emergence of left-wing candidates in certain major
cities.

These struggles have at times succeeded in curbing, altering or delegitimising
certain policies of Trump’s. They have also revealed the existence, within
American society itself, of a deep-seated conflict between an authoritarian,
nationalist and reactionary agenda, and democratic, egalitarian and
internationalist aspirations.

**Women’s mobilisations for the right to abortion**

As soon as Trump arrived at the White House in January 2017, millions of women
took to the streets as part of the _Women’s March_ , organised the day after
his inauguration. This movement was one of the largest mobilisations in US
history. It expressed rejection of Trump’s sexism, his misogynistic remarks
and his desire to undermine reproductive rights.

The _Women’s March_ in January 2017 remains one of the largest demonstrations
in US history, with an estimated turnout of between three and five million
people. It immediately demonstrated that Trump’s election had sparked mass
opposition, particularly amongst women, minorities and progressive movements.

The issue of abortion took centre stage when the Supreme Court – bolstered by
Trump’s appointments of conservative justices – overturned the _Roe v. Wade_
ruling in June 2022, during Joe Biden’s term of office. This ruling had
guaranteed the constitutional right to abortion since 1973. This decision
sparked a wave of protests across the country and contributed to a strong
electoral mobilisation in favour of candidates supporting the right to
abortion.

In response to the overturning of the _Roe v. Wade_ ruling in June 2022 by the
Supreme Court, which was influenced by Trump and his camp, the American
electorate was called upon to vote directly on abortion in sixteen states
between 2022 and 2024. In thirteen of these, the side in favour of maintaining
or extending the right to abortion won the vote, including in several
conservative states such as Kansas, Kentucky, Montana, Ohio, Missouri and
Arizona. These results show that the desire to criminalise abortion does not
enjoy uniform majority support amongst the American electorate and that it
provokes significant popular resistance, including in Republican strongholds.

As such, the defence of women’s rights has become one of the main focal points
of opposition to Trump and Trumpism.

**Environmental and scientific protests**

The _March for Science_ , held in April 2017, was a direct response to Trump’s
climate scepticism and his attacks on federal scientific agencies. Around one
million people took part in demonstrations in more than six hundred towns and
cities, denouncing the questioning of scientific data on climate change.

The _People’s Climate March_ , also in 2017, brought together around 200,000
people in Washington and several hundred thousand across the country. It
protested against the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and policies
favouring the fossil fuel industry.

**Protests against gun violence**

Following the Parkland shooting in Florida in February 2018, the _March for
Our Lives_ movement mobilised between one and two million people, mainly young
people. More than 800 demonstrations took place across all fifty states. This
movement challenged Trump’s support for the gun lobby, the _National Rifle
Association_(NRA), and helped to make gun control a major political issue.

**Teachers’ strikes**

The teachers’ strikes of 2018 and 2019 marked a turning point in American
social struggles. More than 500,000 teaching and school staff took part in
strike action across several states, many of which are conservative. These
protests called for pay rises, better funding for state education and a
reduction in educational inequalities.

**Black Lives Matter and the fight against systemic racism**

The _Black Lives Matter_ movement, which emerged in the wake of police
violence against African Americans, reached its peak in 2020 following the
murder of George Floyd by a police officer in Minneapolis. The _Black Lives
Matter_ movement represented the largest wave of mobilisation in recent
American history. Following the murder of George Floyd in May 2020, protests
took place in over two thousand towns and cities. Some studies estimate that
between fifteen and twenty-six million people took part in at least one
protest, which would make it the largest protest movement in US history.

Trump responded by adopting a confrontational stance. He labelled some
protesters ‘thugs’ and threatened to deploy the army against the
demonstrations. This response reinforced the perception of a president who
supports a militarised police force and refuses to acknowledge the existence
of systemic racism.

_Black Lives Matter_ has, however, achieved significant progress: the scrutiny
of certain police practices, debates on police funding, the removal of racist
symbols in several cities, and the inclusion of the issue of structural racism
in the national political debate.

**After 6 January 2021**

The storming of the Capitol by Trump’s supporters on 6 January 2021 sparked a
wave of protests in defence of democracy. Demonstrations took place in many
American cities to condemn the attempt to overturn the result of the 2020
presidential election and to demand the protection of democratic institutions.

**Solidarity with Palestine**

The Palestinian question has become another major area of internal resistance.
During Trump’s first term, the recognition of Jerusalem as the capital of
Israel in 2017, followed by the relocation of the US embassy, sparked strong
opposition amongst sections of American society.

This opposition intensified from 2023 onwards with Israel’s genocidal war
against Gaza, a war which received active support from Joe Biden’s Democratic
administration. The movement continued during Trump’s second term. Hundreds of
thousands of people demonstrated in major US cities to denounce US military
and diplomatic support for Israel.

University campuses have played a central role. Students have organised sit-
ins, occupations and divestment campaigns targeting companies linked to the
Israeli military-industrial complex. Despite often brutal repression, these
protests have helped to shift the public debate: for the first time in
decades, a significant proportion of American youth are openly questioning
Washington’s unconditional support for Israel.

Mobilisations in solidarity with Palestine reached unprecedented levels from
2023 onwards. On the largest days of action, several hundred thousand people
demonstrated simultaneously in major US cities. University sit-ins spread to
over a hundred universities and colleges, directly involving tens of thousands
of students and leading to hundreds of arrests.

**Protests against ICE and immigration policies**

Trump’s immigration policies also sparked massive resistance. As early as
2017, protests against _the ‘Muslim_ Ban’ – which barred entry to nationals of
several predominantly Muslim countries – swept through US airports.

The separation of thousands of migrant children from their parents at the
border with Mexico sparked international outrage. The _‘Families Belong_
Together’ movement organised large-scale demonstrations to demand the
reunification of families.

During his second term, protests against ICE (_Immigration and Customs
Enforcement_) intensified in response to raids, deportations and detention
centres for migrants. Solidarity networks were set up in several cities to
protect people facing deportation and to document abuses committed by the
immigration authorities. These actions mobilised several hundred thousand
people on an ongoing basis in more than 16 major cities and hundreds of rural
or suburban towns.

Thousands of actions relating to migrants’ rights and opposition to ICE have
been recorded across all 50 states. If we include the _No Kings_ protests (see
below), more than 10 million people have taken part in street demonstrations
to denounce anti-migrant policies and ICE’s methods.

**The ‘No Kings’ movement**

The _‘No_ Kings’ movement emerged as a direct response to Trump’s
authoritarian excesses. It condemns the concentration of presidential power,
attacks on democratic institutions, threats against the media and the desire
to govern by decree.

The _‘No_ Kings’ protests brought together citizens of diverse political
persuasions, united by their refusal to see the United States move towards an
increasingly authoritarian regime. This movement served as a reminder that the
defence of democratic freedoms remains a central issue in the resistance to
Trumpism.

The _No Kings_ movement is one of the most significant expressions of
opposition to Trump’s second term. The main national days of mobilisation,
particularly in 2026, brought together, according to estimates, between three
and five million people in more than 1,500 towns and cities. This scale makes
it one of the largest anti-Trump mobilisations since the _Women’s March_ of
2017.

Here are three key dates in the _No Kings_ mobilisations:

> \+ 14 June 2025 (No Kings 1.0): Around 5 million people across more than
> 2,100 locations.
>
> \+ 18 October 2025 (No Kings 2.0): Around 7 million people at over 2,700
> venues.
>
> \+ 28 March 2026 (No Kings 3.0): Around 8 million people gathered at over
> 3,300 venues.

**LGBTQ+ protests**

Trump’s policies aimed at restricting the rights of transgender people,
particularly in the armed forces and in certain areas of public life, have met
with strong opposition. Between 2022 and 2026, protests against anti-trans
laws brought together tens of thousands, and even hundreds of thousands, of
people on certain national days of action.

**Trade union and social resistance**

We must not overlook the role of trade unions and social movements. The years
2021–2026 were marked by a resurgence of labour struggles in the United
States: strikes in the automotive industry, ‘ ’ in the service sector, at
Amazon warehouses, in Starbucks cafés and in the education sector.

These protests often went beyond wage demands to denounce social inequalities,
job insecurity and the excessive power of large corporations. They
demonstrated that a significant section of the American working class
identifies with neither the Democratic Party’s neoliberalism nor Trump’s
reactionary nationalism.

**Electoral successes of the left: the case of Zohran Mamdani**

Resistance to Trump is not limited to street protests. It is also expressed in
the electoral arena, notably through the emergence of left-wing candidates in
certain major cities.

The case of Zohran Mamdani is particularly significant. A member of _the
Democratic Socialists of America_(DSA), he won the Democratic primaries for
the New York mayoral election, defeating candidates backed by the Democratic
Party _establishment_. He was elected mayor of New York in November 2025
despite threats from Trump and a campaign waged against him by 26 US
billionaires who, according to _Forbes_ magazine, spent over 22 million
dollars to prevent him from being elected. Fortunately, the will and energy of
the people, particularly among the younger generation, triumphed over the
power of money and capital.

His campaign, centred on affordable housing, free public transport, taxation
of great wealth and solidarity with Palestine, mobilised a large section of
the youth and the working classes. It demonstrated that a left-wing political
alternative can emerge in the United States, despite the weight of the two-
party system and the influence of money in election campaigns.

Mamdani’s success is part of a broader trend, which includes the victories of
figures such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar and other
progressive elected representatives. This American left remains in the
minority, but it represents a growing force capable of challenging both
Trumpism and the centrist tendencies of the Democratic Party.

**A multifaceted resistance**

Internal resistance within the United States shows that Trump’s political
agenda faces deep-seated and enduring opposition.

If we take these various waves of mobilisation together, we can see that tens
of millions of people have, at one time or another, taken part in protest
actions against Trump’s policies or against the authoritarian, racist,
patriarchal, warmongering and neoliberal tendencies of Trumpism.

These movements do not form a homogeneous bloc, but constitute a mosaic of
resistance that cuts across the whole of American society: women, African
Americans, Latin Americans, students, workers, scientists, academics,
environmental activists, LGBTQ+ rights advocates and supporters of democracy.

These protests have at times achieved tangible victories, but they also face
growing repression, the power of the conservative media and the country’s
political polarisation. Symbolic of this repression, Renee Nicole Good and
Alex Pretti, who were attempting to intervene during operations against
migrants in Minneapolis, were both killed by ICE officers.

Nevertheless, these movements are fundamental to understanding the limits of
Trump’s power. They serve as a reminder that, even at the heart of the world’s
leading imperialist power, there are social and political forces that
challenge authoritarianism, racism, patriarchy, militarism and neoliberal
policies.

Thus, the history of Trumpism cannot be written solely from the perspective of
the White House. It must also be told through the lens of the millions of
people who, on the streets, on campuses, in workplaces and at the ballot box,
have resisted and continue to resist his political agenda.
